claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

In GeoDeploy's design, the TypeScript app does the math and never makes judgment calls; Jev decides region and modules and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy's Pulumi Automation API step runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and won't run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot occur by construction in GeoDeploy.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates in a single call.
GeoDeploy's single Jev call asks for one selection, five quality scores, two hard noul checks (residency, capacity), and a fallback choice.
GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/questions.ts imports choice, noul, and score from @typesafe-ai/sdk.
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.
The TypeSafeClient has a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with fields like selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain, with the listed weights.
Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier; cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR).

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new cluster region 0.90 (top three flagged for human); existing stack region 0.75 (keep existing); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path).
GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/engine.ts contains the residency hard gate, and each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, answers).

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic price comparison across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

In self-driving mode (`geodeploy monitor`), the agent periodically checks CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up, scale-down, shift, plus a disruption-risk check; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic per-region rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The link /automation/ points to a Pulumi Automation API page that exists.
